From the Gospel accounts: Matthew 28:1-10 - The women witness the empty tomb and the risen Christ speaking in a garden outside Jerusalem. Mary Magdalene alone sees Jesus twice (John 20:11-18), touching him and seeing through her hair, fulfilling Jewish custom regarding touch of the dead. Greek text: ἐγείρω (egeirō, G1453), 'to raise,' is used in Matthew 28:19 where God raises 'whom my Father has raised.' John 20:24-29 - Thomas, after seeing and touching the risen Jesus, proclaims, "My Lord and my God!" (ὁ κύριος μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου). Luke 24:36-43 - The ascended Jesus eats a fish so the disciples know the resurrected body can consume physical nourishment. 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 provides the earliest creedal summary: "For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve (BSB)." This creed, attributed to Paul even among skeptical scholars like N.T. Wright, predates the Gospels. The resurrection is not a mystery (ἀποκρυφία) but a historical fact (κατὰ δύναμιν τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης φύσεως). As James D.G. Dunn demonstrates in "The Historical Jesus," the apostles' transformation from cowards to martyrs demanding death stems directly from encountering the risen Christ, a testimony affirmed by early church historians like Tacitus who noted the Christian riots in Rome. Paul describes appearances to over 500 witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:6), and Mark explicitly records the appearances to Mary Magdalene and the Twelve (Mark 16:9-14). The accounts are consistent across the four Gospels yet contain different details, indicating separate, independent eyewitness reports. The early church leaders—Peter in Jerusalem, Stephen before the Sanhedrin, Paul before King Agrippa—all testify to witnessing the risen Jesus during the trial and execution. No such testimony emerged from their opponents, suggesting this was the most compelling historical claim ever made. "As for the resurrection of the dead, it is a mystery" (1 Corinthians 15:51 BSB). However, this verse acknowledges the mystery while affirming that 'we believe that Jesus of Nazareth was raised from the dead' (Romans 4:25 BSB). results.question: Why does the Bible say suffering exists if God is good?
results.expected_answer: Scripture traces suffering to humanity's fall into sin (Genesis 3, Romans 5:12), which broke the good world God created. Yet the Bible also teaches that God is present in suffering (Psalm 34:18), can bring good out of it (Romans 8:28, Genesis 50:20), and will ultimately end it (Revelation 21:4). Job wrestles honestly with unexplained suffering without receiving a full philosophical answer, but with an encounter with God himself (Job 38-42).
results.response: The Bible addresses the tension between God's goodness and suffering by revealing a theological framework that explains suffering exists as part of God's sovereign plan. This perspective distinguishes between God's immediate benevolence and His ultimate purpose in a fallen world. First, the Bible affirms God's complete goodness as foundational: "I am the LORD, who creates the heavens... whose works are perfect, whose way is just; in all his commandments he delights" – Isaiah 46:10 (BSB). God's character is immutable goodness. Second, the Bible explains suffering by portraying it as a divine gift and discipline. Paul references this paradox: "Not only that! But we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character; and character, hope" – Romans 5:3–4 (BSB). The Greek term for "produces" (karpos, Strong's G2590) indicates suffering yields intrinsic spiritual fruit. Third, the Bible clarifies that suffering is not pointless but is used for sanctification and testimony. Peter teaches: "In the same way, you also rejoice, though a trial for the test of your faith, which is called hope, may cause grief to your persecutors" – 1 Peter 1:6 (BSB). The apostle further emphasizes that Christ endured suffering to secure believers' salvation: "Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous... that he might bring you to God" – 1 Peter 3:18 (BSB). Fourth, Reformed theologian Louis Berkhof observes that suffering often serves as the means by which God's invisible attributes – His faithfulness, love, and sovereignty – are made manifestly known. The Westminster Shorter Catechism summarizes that humanity's chief purpose is "to glorify God and to enjoy him forever," which is accomplished through both suffering and blessing. **Where traditions differ:** Catholic and Orthodox traditions emphasize the **Theosis (Deification)** perspective, where suffering can draw believers into closer communion with God through participation in Christ's redemptive process. Protestant traditions, following John Calvin, emphasize the **Elective Grace** model where God sovereignly ordains all things, including suffering, to conform believers to the image of Christ through the Spirit's work. Augustine comprehensively argued against dualistic views in "The City of God," demonstrating that God's permissive will can encompass suffering if it contributes to His eternal glory and human redemption. **Relevant Greek term:** - **Τειραπορία** (treis apostrophe, Strong's G5016): trial or testing, derived from τειρω (to thresh) implying separation of "chaff" from "grain" in refining process (James 1:2–3).<end_of_turn> <unused56>
